results.title: (PDF) Representation of measurement error in marketing variables: Review of approaches and extension to three-facet designs
results.content: This paper explores approaches for modeling measurement error in marketing research, including random, method and measure specific sources of error. The following approaches are considered: classic confirmatory factor analysis, second-order models, panel models, additive trait-method models, correlated uniqueness models, covariance components analysis, additive trait-method-measure specific-error models, and the direct product model, where traits and methods interact. Method error, including halo effects and social desirability distortions, often contributes to systematic error, potentially leading to distorted measures of consumer perceptions and satisfaction (Bagozzi et al., 1999). Confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) models test hypotheses regarding the latent structure of measures versus observed variables, providing diagnostics for construct validity (Bagozzi et al., 1999). The comparative validity of measures can be drastically influenced by the underlying methods, which may lead to distinct trait variance accounting for observed measures (Bagozzi et al., 1999). The three-facet multiplicative model indicated that attitudes remained stable across time with low to moderate method error, suggesting minimal variance between the traits measured (Bagozzi et al., 1999).

Title: Many IVs estimation of dynamic panel regression models with measurement error - ScienceDirect
# Many IVs estimation of dynamic panel regression models with measurement error☆. In this paper, we investigate a dynamic linear panel regression model with measurement error. In this paper we investigate the effect of measurement error on the estimation of a dynamic linear panel model when we use instrumental variables. We consider the 2SLSE mainly because it is the most frequently used IV estimator and simple to compute, although the 2SLSE is not an efficient estimator for a dynamic panel regression with measurement error. AA investigated the simple dynamic linear panel regression model with fixed effects, but not allowing for measurement error, when are large. The presence of measurement error creates serial dependence among the (composite) error terms in the dynamic panel regression, so that our estimation requires different sets of IVs from those of AA. The second contribution of the paper is to investigate how to reduce (or correct) the asymptotic bias of the two 2SLSEs due to many IVs. For this, in this paper we consider the jackknife instrumental variable estimation (JIVE) of Phillips and Hale (1977) and Angrist et al. However, compared to ours, Akashi and Kunitomo (2012) did not allow for measurement error in their model and so did not consider a bias-corrected estimation. In Section 2 we introduce a simple dynamic panel regression model and measurement error. In Section 3 we introduce two transformations of the panel data model to eliminate fixed effects and discuss the IVs. Section 4 investigates asymptotics of the 2SLS estimator based on the IVs of Section 2. In the conventional dynamic panel regression model where the error term does not have serial correlation, this problem disappears when is large (e.g., see Hahn et al., 2002). In the previous sections, we discussed that the 2SLS estimators based on both forward demeaning and first difference are asymptotically biased for the estimation of the dynamic panel model with measurement error. In this section, we investigate the finite sample properties of the 2SLS and JIVE estimations for the simple dynamic model with measurement error based on a simple Monte Carlo simulation design. ### GMM estimation in panel data models with measurement error.

results.title: Full article: Estimating Measurement Error in Longitudinal Data Using the Longitudinal MultiTrait MultiError Approach
results.content: Nevertheless, most of the statistical methods developed for estimating measurement error either consider only one type of measurement error at a time (such as the quasi-simplex model, Alwin, Citation2007; Cernat et al., Citation2021) or need extra data for validation (such as the longitudinal vignettes and the combined Hidden Markov Chain, Paccagnella, Citation2021; Pavlopoulos et al., Citation2021). By implementing the newly developed MultiTrait MultiError (MTME, Cernat & Oberski, Citation2019, Citation2021) in a longitudinal study we are able to separate four source of measurement error: social desirability, acquiescence, method effects and random error. A number of approaches have been developed to estimate and correct for such errors, such as latent variable modelling (e.g., Alwin, Citation2007; Bollen, Citation1989; Saris & Gallhofer, Citation2007), data collection experiments (e.g., Tourangeau et al., Citation2000), anchoring vignettes (e.g., King et al., Citation2003) or data integration (e.g., Oberski et al., Citation2017; Pavlopoulos et al., Citation2021). The model postulates a measurement model using a latent variable approach as well as an auto-regressive structural part that enables the estimation of change in time of the trait, or “true score.” With at least three waves of data the model can be estimated, albeit with some strong assumptions: random error or the variance of the residual is constant in time. They further show how it is possible to construct a statistical model that concurrently estimates the different sources of measurement error in a latent variable framework using survey experiments. Cernat and Oberski (Citation2021) show how it is possible to use such a design to estimate concurrently four sources of measurement error in six questions measuring attitudes to immigration: social desirability, acquiescence, method effect and random error. To understand individual level change in measurement error we estimate the LMTME model, which includes a measurement model at each wave, concurrently, as well as the stability of the latent variables. In addition to the insights regarding the stability of correlated measurement error over time the LMTME model also makes it possible to correct for measurement error by estimating change in time using the trait variables instead of the observed variables. Using this design we can separate five sources of variation in questions measuring attitudes towards immigration: trait, random error, social desirability, acquiescence and method effect.
